item.title: Policy Brief 2: Closing the Coordination Loop
item.dc:creator: D2P Project Team
item.description:
ImportantFor Decision-Makers

Target audience: Ministerial Advisory Committee (MAC), National Department of Health (NDoH), DALRRD Pesticide Registrar, Provincial Health Leadership.

Companion briefs: Surveillance · Terbufos restriction.

1. Policy question

Should NDoH and DALRRD mandate a closed-loop coordination workflow — where every NMC notification triggers an investigation that is recorded on NMC, every EHP→DALRRD referral is structured, and every DALRRD action is fed back to NICD and the clinician?

2. Public health problem

Better detection (see the Surveillance brief) is wasted if the system does not act on what it detects. South Africa’s pesticide-poisoning response chain has eight sequential decision points between “case suspected” and “regulatory action closes the loop”, and six of those eight default to a broken-loop terminal. A correctly-notified case can still produce no investigation, no source removal, and no regulatory follow-up — leaving the underlying hazard in place and producing predictable secondary cases.

3. Status quo

NoteCanonical model parameters (auto-loaded from the Parameters Hub)

All numerical claims in this brief draw from a single CSV — amua_import_parameters_v3.csv — rendered in full at the Parameters Hub. The headline values below are pulled from that file at render time; do not edit the numbers in this brief — edit the CSV and re-render.

Who bears the R2.34B annual burden?

Annual burden by stakeholder (headline scenario, ZAR 2025)

Stakeholder Value Share
NDoH — public hospitals (UPFS ward + ICU + drugs) R70.00 million 3%
NHLS — laboratory (BChE, GC-MS, repeat clinical chemistry) R10.00 million 0%

TOTAL R2.34 billion 100%

Reading the table. ~96 % of the R2.34B is mortality, borne by households and the wider economy as lost lifetime earnings (1,500 deaths × R1.5M human-capital, undiscounted; sensitivity: R1.05M at 3 % discount). The directly-budgeted health-sector share is R80M (NDoH ~R70M hospital + NHLS ~R10M lab) — modest in absolute terms, but it is the only column that appears on a departmental budget line. DALRRD bears R0 of the burden side by construction: their cost sits on the intervention side (enforcement, recalls, registration action).

For the full sourced parameter set (CFR by severity, UPFS tariffs, per-option costs, induced-demand components, DALY monetisation, NMB), see the Parameters Hub. For the v2 → v3 critical appraisal, see parameter_appraisal.qmd.

NoteWho bears the R2.34B — the whole-of-government picture

The burden is split asymmetrically across government and society: NDoH ~R70M (3 %), NHLS ~R10M (<1 %), individuals/households ~R10M out-of-pocket (<1 %), and ~R2.25B in lost lifetime earnings (96 %) borne by households and the wider economy. DALRRD bears no direct burden-side cost — but they hold the only legal lever that prevents the underlying exposure. That asymmetry is exactly why the coordination loop must terminate in DALRRD action, not just in EHP investigation: the agency carrying the lowest share of the burden controls the highest-leverage intervention, so closing the NICD → EHP → DALRRD loop is the cheapest cross-departmental coordination available to government.

The notification pathway — one-way and broken

Reading the diagram. Clinicians do file on NMC — that is the formal entry point. NMC does SMS the local EHP, who is mandated to investigate. The chain breaks at two specific places: (a) the EHP investigation outcome is never written back to NMC because no NMC field requires it; and (b) the EHP→DALRRD referral, when it happens, is informal and likewise unrecorded. DALRRD action — if any — flows back to the EHP at best, and never to NICD or the originating clinician.

4. Root cause analysis

The five drivers are: (1) NMC schema lacks a closure-of-loop field; (2) EHP→DALRRD referral has no SOP; (3) DALRRD has no inbound NICD intelligence feed despite a formal request for one; (4) clinicians get no case-status feedback so the notification has no perceived value; (5) no decision node in the chain has an accountable owner with a KPI, so nothing fails loudly when the loop breaks.

5. Policy options

Option C1 — Mandate an NMC closure-of-loop field for EHPs

Add a structured “investigation outcome” field to NMC against every notification: visited/not visited, source identified/not, environmental sampling done/not, referral made/not. Make completion within 14 days an EHP performance KPI. No new legislation; an NMC schema change and circular from NDoH. Annual cost: ~R30,000 (schema update + training material).

Option C2 — Structured EHP→DALRRD referral form on NMC

Add a referral form to NMC that auto-emails the DALRRD Pesticide Registrar/Inspectorate when an EHP suspects an unsafe product, illegal sale, or occupational source. Captures product, location, suspected agent, severity, and EHP contact. Replaces today’s informal phone/email referral. Annual cost: ~R25,000.

Option C3 — NICD→DALRRD poisoning intelligence feed (★ recommended)

DALRRD has formally requested poisoning intelligence to inform registration, labelling, and inspectorate priorities. Output: a quarterly NICD brief by suspected product / geography / season, plus an ad-hoc cluster-alert channel. Closes the regulator-feedback gap and gives DALRRD the evidence base for product-specific action (the explicit prerequisite for the Terbufos brief recommendation). Annual cost: ~R40,000 (NICD analyst + DALRRD liaison), 12 weeks.

Option C4 — Auto-feedback to notifying clinician

NMC sends the notifying clinician a quarterly case-status summary: outcome of EHP investigation, regulatory action taken, whether their case contributed to a detected cluster. Removes the “I notify into a black hole” disincentive. Annual cost: ~R20,000 (templating + email integration).

Option C5 — Joint KPI dashboard

A small public dashboard tracking: median time from notification to EHP investigation; % of notifications with a recorded outcome; % of clusters with documented DALRRD action; % of notifying clinicians who received feedback. Co-owned by NICD, DALRRD, and provincial DoHs. Annual cost: ~R30,000.

Coordination Full Package (C1 + C2 + C3 + C4 + C5)

Total annual cost of the Coordination Full Package: ~R145,000. No new legislation required.

6. Decision tree — coordination outcomes per suspected case

6a. Where the chain breaks today

Joint P(loop fully closes) ≈ 1.1 % under the status quo. Expected coordination cost per suspected case ≈ R196,400 — virtually the full per-case societal burden of R197,000, because the loop almost never closes.

6b. Clinical-outcome subtree

Each coordination terminal feeds into a clinical-outcome subtree for the index case and for the secondary cases that would otherwise follow from the same source:

6c. What changes under each coordination scenario

Burden avoided is split by who would otherwise have borne it, so each agency sees the share of the win that flows back to its own budget line or constituency. The avoided-burden split uses the same shares as the canonical stakeholder table above: ~3.4 % health sector (NDoH + NHLS), ~96.6 % households (mortality + OOP).

Modelled coordination outcomes at national scale (× 11,690 suspected cases/year). Stakeholder columns apply the canonical share table (NDoH+NHLS = R80M of R2.34B; households = R2.26B of R2.34B) to the total avoided burden in each scenario. Probabilities are placeholders aligned with the surveillance detection-rate ranges in the Surveillance brief.
Scenario P(loop closed) Deaths averted / yr Avoided — health system (NDoH + NHLS) Avoided — households (mortality + OOP) Total avoided
Status quo 1.1 % 15 — — —
+ C3 (NICD→DALRRD feed) ~40 % ~547 ~R29M ~R806M ~R835M
Coordination Full Package (C1–C5) ~70 % ~957 ~R50M ~R1,400M ~R1,450M

Reading by audience.

  • NDoH / NHLS: the R50M avoided on your budget line is ~330× the R145k Full-Package operating cost — a credible business case even before counting household mortality.
  • DALRRD: you do not bear the R2.34B, but C3 is the lowest-cost route to the evidence base you need for product-specific action (see Terbufos brief).
  • Treasury / Presidency: ~R1.4B/yr of household and societal cost is structurally retired; this is the cross-departmental coordination return that justifies the joint DG circular.

7. Implementation considerations

Component Lead agency Year-1 cost Critical path
C1: NMC closure-of-loop field NICD NMC team + NDoH circular R30k NMC schema change; EHP training
C2: Structured DALRRD referral form on NMC NICD + DALRRD Pesticide Registrar R25k DALRRD inbox + workflow
C3: NICD→DALRRD intelligence feed NICD analyst + DALRRD liaison R40k Quarterly brief template; cluster alert SOP
C4: Notifier auto-feedback NICD NMC team R20k Email templating
C5: Joint KPI dashboard NICD + DALRRD + Provinces R30k KPI definitions; public hosting
Total NICD-led ~R145k All within existing legal authority

Institutional mechanism. A quarterly Joint Coordination Forum (NICD chair; DALRRD, NHLS, PIH, and one rotating provincial DoH representative) reviews the KPI dashboard, signs off cluster-alert escalations, and resolves cross-departmental blockers. Mandated by joint NDoH–DALRRD Director-General circular. No new legislation required.

Risks and mitigations.

  • EHP non-compliance with new NMC field. Mitigation: 14-day completion KPI tied to provincial performance reviews; circular from NDoH DG.
  • DALRRD capacity to act on referrals. Mitigation: C3 quarterly brief lets DALRRD prioritise by burden rather than respond reactively.
  • Privacy concerns on clinician auto-feedback. Mitigation: feedback is aggregate at clinician level, not patient-identifying.

8. Recommended next step

Adopt C1 + C3 as the Coordination MVP, and the Full Package within 12 months.

  • Weeks 1–4: NDoH–DALRRD joint DG circular committing to the closed-loop model; standing up the Joint Coordination Forum.
  • Weeks 4–12: C1 NMC schema change + EHP training; C3 NICD→DALRRD quarterly brief begins on the existing NMC data.
  • Months 3–12: C2 referral form, C4 auto-feedback, C5 KPI dashboard go live.
  • Month 12: Evaluate against (i) median notification-to-investigation time, (ii) % of notifications with recorded outcome, (iii) DALRRD-reported regulatory actions per quarter.

The surveillance signal that flows into this loop is covered in the Surveillance brief. The first product-specific regulatory action the loop should be designed to deliver is the subject of the Terbufos brief.

item.dc:creator: D2P Project Team
item.description:
1 Executive Summary

This document provides detailed cost estimates for implementing and operating improved pesticide poisoning surveillance in South Africa. All estimates are based on:

  • Current government salary scales (2025/2026)
  • NHLS IT infrastructure costs (confirmed with NHLS IT management)
  • Provincial health department operating budgets
  • Expert elicitation for liaison and coordination activities
ImportantHeadline Findings — Two Cost Lenses

Narrow government-provider cost (NICD/NHLS/PIH/Provincial DoH coordination only): ~R237,000/year.

Pressure-tested whole-system cost (including downstream hospital toxicology workload, lab test volume, Environmental Health Practitioner (EHP) investigations, and agricultural enforcement): ~R1.55 million/year (range: R0.9–2.7 million).

Why the gap matters: Improved surveillance is not free at the point of detection. Every BChE auto-notification triggers a clinical work-up, a confirmatory test, an EHP follow-up, and — for hotspots — DALRRD enforcement. The narrow figure understates true budget impact by ~6×. Decision-makers should plan for the comprehensive figure to avoid stranding the programme without operational capacity.

For context, the comprehensive figure still represents:

  • 0.0028% of the National Department of Health budget (~R56 billion/year)
  • R172 per severe pesticide poisoning case (based on ~9,000 cases/year)
  • Less than the salary of 3 mid-level epidemiologists

2 Costing Methodology

2.1 Two Costing Perspectives

This analysis uses two nested perspectives to make the trade-offs transparent:

  1. Narrow government-provider perspective (the original estimate, ~R237k/year). Captures only the costs borne by:
    • National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD)
    • National Health Laboratory Service (NHLS) — coordination only
    • Poisons Information Helpline (PIH)
    • Provincial Departments of Health — coordination only
  2. Pressure-tested whole-system perspective (Section Pressure-Testing the Costs). Adds the induced demand that improved surveillance creates downstream:
    • Hospitals: clinician time for exposure histories, sample collection, NMC notification completion, and data collation by records clerks
    • Laboratories: higher BChE test volumes, confirmatory GC-MS toxicology, sample transport and storage
    • Environmental Health Practitioners (EHPs): field investigation of clusters, environmental sampling, source tracing
    • Agricultural enforcement: DALRRD compliance officers responding to illegal-pesticide signals, retailer audits, registration follow-up

Still excluded (for now):

  • Patient out-of-pocket costs and productivity losses
  • Wider societal costs (community engagement, media)
  • Capital depreciation on existing NHLS lab equipment
WarningWhy This Matters

The narrow perspective is appropriate for “what new line items appear in the surveillance programme budget?” — but it understates the real fiscal impact on the health and agriculture system. A surveillance system that detects more cases necessarily generates more downstream work. Failing to budget for it leads to: (a) overworked frontline staff, (b) backlogs in lab confirmation, (c) un-investigated hotspots, and (d) erosion of the system within 12–18 months.

2.2 Time Horizon

  • Pilot phase: 6 months (Q3–Q4 2026)
  • Ongoing operations: Annual costs for steady-state implementation

2.3 Currency and Inflation

  • All costs in South African Rand (ZAR)
  • Based on 2025/2026 fiscal year salary scales and price levels
  • No inflation adjustment (costs represent current purchasing power)

3.7 Full Package: All Options Combined

4 Pressure-Testing the Costs: Downstream Demand on the Whole System

The narrow estimates above (~R237k/year) capture only the surveillance coordination layer — NICD, NHLS liaison, PIH reporting, provincial coordinators. But improved surveillance is not cost-neutral to the wider health and agriculture system. Every additional BChE notification triggers:

  1. Hospital response: Clinician time to complete exposure histories, order confirmatory tests, fill out NMC forms, liaise with EHPs. Records clerks collate the data.
  2. Laboratory testing: Higher volume of BChE screening tests (as awareness spreads), confirmatory GC-MS toxicology for hotspots, sample transport logistics.
  3. Environmental Health Practitioner (EHP) investigations: Field visits to suspected exposure sites, environmental sampling (water, soil, food), source tracing, retailer inspections.
  4. Agricultural enforcement: DALRRD compliance officers investigate illegal pesticide sales, conduct product recalls, audit registration status.

This section quantifies the induced demand from the Full Package (Options 1–5 combined).

4.1 Downstream Cost Component 1: Hospital Toxicology Workload

Scenario: Full Package detects 85% of hotspots (vs. 45% today). This means ~40% more severe cases are actively followed up by hospitals (not just passively recorded). Each follow-up requires:

4.1.2 Hospital Consumables & Data Systems

4.2 Downstream Cost Component 2: Laboratory Testing Volume Escalation

Scenario: Improved surveillance increases demand for BChE screening tests (as clinicians become more aware) and confirmatory GC-MS toxicology for hotspots.

4.2.1 Increased BChE Screening Volume

4.2.2 Confirmatory GC-MS Toxicology for Hotspots

4.2.3 Sample Transport & Storage

Total laboratory downstream costs: ~R493,000/year

4.3 Downstream Cost Component 3: Environmental Health Practitioner (EHP) Investigations

Scenario: Full Package detects 3.8 additional hotspots/year. Each hotspot triggers an EHP field investigation — site visit, environmental sampling (water, soil, food), source tracing, retailer inspection.

4.3.1 EHP Personnel Time

4.3.2 Environmental Sampling & Analysis

4.3.3 EHP Travel & Reporting

Total EHP downstream costs: ~R154,000/year

4.4 Downstream Cost Component 4: Agricultural Enforcement (DALRRD)

Scenario: Environmental sampling identifies illegal pesticide sales or misuse of restricted products in ~50% of hotspots. DALRRD compliance officers must investigate retailers, audit registration status, and coordinate product recalls.

4.4.1 DALRRD Compliance Officer Workload

DALRRD personnel: ~R89,000/year

4.4.2 Product Sampling & Testing

Product testing: ~R20,000/year

4.4.3 Legal & Administrative Costs

Legal & admin: ~R12,000/year

Total DALRRD enforcement costs: ~R121,000/year

4.5 Pressure-Tested Full Package: Comprehensive System Costs

ImportantComprehensive System Cost: ~R1.19 Million/Year

The pressure-tested comprehensive figure is 5.0× higher than the narrow surveillance coordination budget. This represents the true fiscal impact on the health and agriculture system.

Key drivers:

  1. Laboratory testing (41% of comprehensive cost): Higher BChE screening volume as awareness spreads
  2. Surveillance coordination (20%): Original narrow estimate (NICD/NHLS/PIH/Provincial DoH)
  3. Hospital workload (16%): Clinician time for 800 additional active case follow-ups
  4. EHP investigations (13%): Field investigations for 3.8 additional hotspots
  5. DALRRD enforcement (10%): Compliance investigations for illegal pesticide sales

4.6 Sensitivity Analysis: Low, Base, and High Scenarios

The comprehensive cost estimate is sensitive to key parameters. Three scenarios:

NoteRecommended Planning Figure

For budgeting purposes, use the BASE scenario: ~R1.19 million/year (range: R715k–R2.0M).

This represents:

  • 0.002% of National DoH budget (~R56 billion)
  • R132 per severe pesticide poisoning case (9,000 cases/year)
  • Less than 3 mid-level epidemiologists’ salaries

Even the HIGH scenario (R2.0M) is 0.004% of NDoH budget — well within affordability thresholds for a national public health priority.

5 Cost Drivers and Assumptions

5.1 Personnel Cost Assumptions

  • Salary scales: Based on 2025/2026 government payscales (OSD levels)
  • Benefits: Not itemized separately (salaries are all-inclusive)
  • FTE allocation: Estimated % of time required for surveillance activities
NoteFTE Allocation Methodology

FTE estimates based on:

  1. Time-and-motion studies from analogous surveillance programs (TB, HIV, COVID-19)
  2. Expert elicitation from NICD/NHLS/PIH staff
  3. Conservative assumptions (overestimate rather than underestimate)

Validation planned: Pilot will track actual staff time to refine estimates.

5.2 IT Cost Assumptions

  • LIS configuration: Based on NHLS IT quote for similar auto-notification rules
  • HL7 middleware: Existing infrastructure (marginal cost only)
  • Maintenance: 10% of development cost per year (industry standard)

5.3 Other Cost Assumptions

  • Travel: R250/km (government rate) × estimated distance
  • Venues: R500/meeting for provincial coordination meetings
  • Sampling kits: R1,000/kit × 10 investigations/year

6 Sensitivity of Costs

6.1 Cost Uncertainty

6.2 Scenario: National Rollout (All 9 Provinces)

Key insight: Options 3 and 4 (BChE auto-notify and PIH reports) are national systems — they cost the same whether implemented in 3 provinces or 9. Only Option 5 (provincial coordination) scales linearly with number of provinces.

7 Budget Impact Analysis

7.1 Annual Budget Comparison

7.2 Cost per Case Averted (Illustrative)

Assuming Full Package prevents even a modest reduction in severe cases:

For comparison:

  • Cost per DALY averted for other public health interventions in South Africa:
    • Insecticide-treated bed nets (malaria): ~R800/DALY
    • HPV vaccination: ~R2,500/DALY
    • Rotavirus vaccination: ~R1,800/DALY

Implication: Even if Full Package prevents only 100 cases/year, it’s comparable to other cost-effective interventions.

8 Funding Sources

8.1 Potential Funding Mechanisms (Comprehensive System Costs)

Potential funding sources for comprehensive system costs
Source Viability Estimated Amount Notes
NDoH central budget High R800,000 Hospital workload, surveillance coordination, lab escalation
NHLS operational budget High R300,000 BChE screening volume, confirmatory toxicology, sample logistics
Provincial conditional grants Medium R200,000 EHP investigations, provincial coordination
DALRRD enforcement budget Medium R120,000 Compliance investigations, product testing, legal costs
Research grants (pilot only) Low R200,000 Non-sustainable; pilot-phase seed funding
NoteMulti-Sectoral Funding is Essential

Unlike the narrow surveillance coordination budget (R237k), the comprehensive system costs (~R1.2M) require buy-in from multiple departments:

  • Department of Health: Hospital workload, lab testing, EHP investigations (~R900k)
  • Department of Agriculture, Land Reform & Rural Development (DALRRD): Compliance enforcement (~R120k)
  • Provincial Health Departments: EHP staffing, field investigations (~R180k)

This is appropriate — pesticide poisoning surveillance is an inter-sectoral problem. Funding should be matched to responsibilities.

8.2 Recommended Funding Strategy (Comprehensive Costs)

Pilot phase (6 months, 3 provinces):

  • Research grant or donor funding: R400,000 (setup costs)
  • NDoH central budget: R300,000
  • NHLS operational budget: R150,000
  • Provincial conditional grants: R100,000
  • Total pilot budget: R950,000

National rollout (ongoing, 3 provinces):

  • NDoH central budget: R800,000/year
  • NHLS operational budget: R300,000/year
  • Provincial conditional grants: R200,000/year
  • DALRRD enforcement budget: R120,000/year
  • Total ongoing (3 provinces): R1.42 million/year

Scale to 9 provinces (Year 3+):

  • Incremental costs for Options 1–4: Minimal (national systems)
  • Incremental costs for Option 5 (EHP investigations): +R300,000 (6 additional provinces)
  • Total national (9 provinces): R1.72 million/year

9 Limitations of Cost Estimates

WarningKey Limitations

Narrow surveillance coordination estimates (R237k):

  1. Placeholder salary data: Based on typical government scales, not confirmed individual salaries
  2. FTE estimates unvalidated: Staff time requirements will be measured during pilot
  3. No scale economies: Assumes linear scaling with number of provinces (may underestimate efficiencies)

Comprehensive system estimates (R1.19M):

  1. Induced demand is modeled, not observed: We assume 20% BChE volume increase and 800 additional active case follow-ups. Actual utilization depends on clinician awareness campaigns, which are uncertain.
  2. Hospital time-per-case assumptions: Based on analogous surveillance programs (TB, HIV), not pesticide-specific time-and-motion studies.
  3. Hotspot-to-enforcement conversion rate: We assume 50% of hotspots trigger DALRRD investigations. Actual rate depends on EHP referral practices and DALRRD capacity, both unknown.
  4. No capacity constraints modeled: Estimates assume NHLS labs, hospital staff, and EHPs can absorb the incremental workload. If capacity is saturated, marginal costs may be higher (require new hires, not just time reallocation).
  5. Geographic variation ignored: Urban hotspots (Gauteng, Western Cape) may have lower investigation costs than rural hotspots (Limpopo, Eastern Cape) due to travel distance. We use national averages.
  6. Exchange rate risk: Lab reagent costs (especially GC-MS reference standards) are import-dependent and subject to ZAR/USD fluctuations.

Both perspectives exclude:

  • Patient out-of-pocket costs and productivity losses
  • Wider societal costs (community education, media engagement)
  • Capital depreciation on existing NHLS lab equipment
  • Opportunity costs (staff time diverted from other surveillance priorities)

10 Next Steps

10.1 Cost Data Collection During Pilot

The pilot will track:

  1. Actual staff time spent on surveillance activities (time logs)
  2. IT development hours for LIS configuration (project management records)
  3. Travel costs for field investigations (expense reports)
  4. Meeting costs (venue hire, catering)

10.2 Cost Model Refinement

Once pilot data are available:

  1. Update FTE estimates with empirical time logs
  2. Adjust IT costs based on actual development hours
  3. Incorporate scale economies if observed
  4. Add uncertainty distributions for probabilistic budget impact analysis

Questions about costing? Contact the D2P team at contact@example.com

1 Introduction

This document describes the decision tree model used to compare five policy options for improving pesticide poisoning surveillance in South Africa. The model was built using Amua (open-source decision analysis software) and validated with extensive sensitivity analyses.

NotePurpose of This Model

Question: Which combination of short-term institutional actions will most efficiently improve hotspot detection and response?

Approach: Compare 6 strategies (status quo + 5 options) on two dimensions:

  1. Effectiveness: Number of hotspots detected and responded to (out of 10/year)
  2. Cost: Annual implementation and operational costs (ZAR)

Output: Cost-effectiveness ratios to inform policy prioritization

2 Model Structure

2.1 Decision Tree Overview

All parameter values are currently PLACEHOLDERS. The model is designed to be updated with real data from the surveillance pilot (launched Q3 2026).

Current estimates are based on:

  • Expert elicitation (NICD, NHLS, PIH staff)
  • International literature on pesticide surveillance systems
  • Analogous infectious disease surveillance programs in South Africa

2.3 Parameters

2.3.1 Baseline Epidemiology

2.3.2 Effectiveness Parameters

Each option has an estimated probability of detecting a hotspot:

2.3.3 Cost Parameters

3 Model Results

3.1 Base-Case Analysis

3.2 Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratios (ICERs)

The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) tells us how much it costs to detect one additional hotspot compared to the next-best option.

TipInterpretation
  • Option 3 (BChE auto-notify) dominates Option 4 — it’s both cheaper and more effective
  • Best value: Option 3 costs ~R57,000 per additional hotspot detected (compared to status quo)
  • Full Package: Costs ~R114,000 per additional hotspot — still reasonable for comprehensive coverage

4 Sensitivity Analysis

4.1 One-Way Sensitivity Analyses

We tested how results change when individual parameters vary:

4.1.1 1. Detection Probability for Option 3 (BChE Auto-Notify)

Key findings:

  • Model is most sensitive to baseline assumptions about total hotspots/year
  • Detection probability has moderate impact
  • Cost variations don’t affect effectiveness (as expected)

4.1.2 2. Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis (PSA)

We ran 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations varying all parameters simultaneously according to their uncertainty distributions:

Key findings:

  • Option 3 and Full Package remain superior to status quo in >95% of simulations
  • Full Package has narrower uncertainty than Option 3 alone (redundancy reduces variance)

4.2 Scenario Analyses

4.2.1 Scenario 1: Pessimistic (Low Effectiveness, High Cost)

Assumptions:

  • Costs doubled

Conclusion: Options remain valuable even if real-world performance is much worse than expected.

4.2.2 Scenario 2: Optimistic (High Effectiveness, Low Cost)

  • Detection probabilities increased by 50%
  • Costs halved

5.1 Face Validity

Model reviewed by:

  • NICD surveillance epidemiologists
  • NHLS laboratory managers
  • PIH clinical toxicologists
  • Academic health economists (UCT School of Public Health)

Feedback incorporated:

  • Adjusted detection probabilities based on expert elicitation
  • Added response success rate as probabilistic node
  • Included scenario for “Option 5 requires Option 3 or 4”

5.2 Internal Validity

  • Parameter consistency: All probabilities sum to 1.0
  • Cost additivity: Full Package cost = sum of individual option costs
  • Effectiveness synergy: Full Package > sum of individual effects (captures coordination benefits)

5.3 External Validity (Pending)

  2. Update cost parameters with actual implementation expenses

  2. Linear effectiveness assumption: Model assumes options combine additively (may underestimate synergies)
  3. No discounting: Costs and effects not discounted over time (justified for short time horizon)
  4. No health outcomes: Model tracks hotspots detected, not deaths/disabilities averted (future extension planned)

ImportantFor Decision-Makers

Target audience: Ministerial Advisory Committee (MAC), National Department of Health (NDoH), Provincial Health Leadership, NICD/NHLS leadership.

Companion briefs: Coordination · Terbufos restriction.

1. Policy question

Should NDoH invest in automated, multi-source pesticide-poisoning surveillance to close the detection gap between the NMC, NHLS laboratory, and PIH data streams?

2. Public health problem

South Africa under-detects pesticide poisoning. Three data streams each see a fraction of the problem; none sees the whole:

  • Most cases never appear in NMC.
  • Severe laboratory results do not trigger a public-health alert.
  • The country’s largest single source of clinical signal — the Poisons Information Helpline — is not used for surveillance at all.

Hotspots are detected late or not at all; clusters from contaminated food, illegal sales, or unsafe occupational exposure run their course before any agency responds; and the country has no real-time view of which products are causing harm.

3. Status quo

NoteCanonical model parameters (auto-loaded from the Parameters Hub)

Reading the table. ~96 % of the R2.34B is mortality, borne by households and the wider economy as lost lifetime earnings (1,500 deaths × R1.5M human-capital, undiscounted; sensitivity: R1.05M at 3 % discount). The directly-budgeted health-sector share is R80M (NDoH ~R70M hospital + NHLS ~R10M lab) — modest in absolute terms, but it is the only column that appears on a departmental budget line. DALRRD bears R0 of the burden side by construction: their cost sits on the intervention side (enforcement, recalls, registration action).

For the full sourced parameter set (CFR by severity, UPFS tariffs, per-option costs, induced-demand components, DALY monetisation, NMB), see the Parameters Hub. For the v2 → v3 critical appraisal, see parameter_appraisal.qmd.

NoteHealth-sector share of the burden — what surveillance unlocks

The public health system bears ~R80M of the R2.34B annual burden directly on its own budget lines — ~R70M to NDoH (UPFS ward + ICU days, ventilation, atropine + PAM) and ~R10M to NHLS (BChE, GC-MS confirmatory volume). Every percentage point of additional detection (Options 1–5 below) reduces ward-days, ICU-days, and repeat lab workload before any mortality benefit is counted — so the surveillance investment pays back on the NDoH and NHLS budget lines first, and on household / societal mortality (~R2.25B) second.

Architecturally, the three streams are unlinked:

What this means in plain numbers. NMC sees ~690 cases/year. NHLS sees ~2,000 severe BChE results/year on live patients but does not auto-notify. PIH receives ~9,000 calls/year that are never aggregated to a surveillance dataset. The true annual burden of ~11,690 cases is therefore observed at < 6 % completeness by NMC alone.

Detection vs. true burden — a critical distinction

Better surveillance has two opposite numerical effects that decision-makers must not confuse:

Effect Direction Driver Interpretation
Observed burden ↑ Better case-finding (auto-notify, MVD ingest) The headline “case count” will rise as detection improves — this is success, not failure.
True burden ↓ Faster source removal, targeted regulation, prevention Number of actual poisonings falls as hotspots are addressed earlier.

A naive reading of post-pilot data will show “more cases” and conclude the system is getting worse. The correct reading is to compare completeness-adjusted true incidence against the baseline, using laboratory and PIH denominators as the closest proxy. This needs to be agreed up front with NDoH and the MAC.

4. Root cause analysis

The four root causes are all executional, not legislative. Each one is already legally permissible under Section 90 of the National Health Act (2003) and the existing NMC regulations.

5. Policy options

Option S1 — Activate the NHLS→NMC IT feed (MOU exists)

The NHLS–NICD MOU for routine BChE data sharing already exists on paper. What is missing is the IT implementation — a working LIS-to-NMC connector (HL7 / structured flat-file export), QA governance, and a monthly reconciliation. Detection rises from ~4.5 to ~5.2 hotspots / 10 (annual cost ~R40k ongoing + ~R80k one-off, 8–12 weeks).

Option S3a — BChE auto-notification (★ recommended — capability exists)

Configure the NHLS LIS to fire an automatic NICD notification when a BChE result shows severe inhibition (< 50 % of normal), within 24 hours of validation. No new test, no new reagent contract — only an IT configuration on top of the ~9,000 BChE tests/year already performed. Detection rises to ~6.7 / 10 for R55k/year in 2–4 weeks. This is the highest-value, fastest option on the menu.

Option S3b — Live-patient chemical toxicology + auto-notification (★ recommended, medium term)

NHLS currently performs chemical toxicology (qualitative/quantitative pesticide assays) post-mortem only. There is no live-patient toxicology capability. Option S3b funds:

  • Phase 1: a sentinel tertiary site (e.g. CHB) to perform live-patient chemical toxicology.
  • Phase 2–3: 4–5 site rollout with auto-notification wired in.

The clinical-surveillance value is agent attribution: S3a tells us a poisoning happened; S3b tells us which product. Without S3b, ~10,000 survivors/year are recorded with agent “unknown / suspected”, which makes targeted regulation (see Terbufos brief) impossible. Cost: ~R1.2M pilot site → ~R3.6M for 5-site rollout, 6–12 months. Funded from research-surveillance streams (SAMRC, Bloomberg, Gates), not the surveillance operating budget.

Option S4 — PIH live dashboard + Minimum Viable Dataset (★ recommended)

Two layers:

  • Short term (1–2 weeks): PIH publishes a live dashboard of pesticide-related calls (counts, geography, agent, severity, demographics). No new data; just a daily extract from existing call records.
  • Medium term (3–9 months): PIH and NICD agree a Minimum Viable Dataset (MVD) so the ~9,000 calls/year can be ingested into NMC as a structured surveillance stream.

Detection rises to ~6.1 / 10 for R62k/year. The dashboard is the lowest-hanging fruit in the whole portfolio: it ships in days.

6. Decision tree — from surveillance investment to averted burden

Cases averted = (P_detect − 0.45) × η × 11,690. Deaths averted = cases averted × p_death (0.13). The MVP package averts ≈ 150 deaths/year for ≈ R157,000 spend — ~R1,000 per death averted against a per-death societal cost of R1.5M.

Privacy & legal. All flows are de-identified (age, sex, facility, result, date). POPIA-compliant under existing Section 90 NHA authority. No new legislation required.

Risks. (i) Low BChE testing uptake by clinicians — S3a fires only on tests ordered. (ii) Data-quality drift if facility metadata is incomplete (geocoding will fail). (iii) Capacity bottleneck at provincial response level — the Coordination brief addresses this.

8. Recommended next step

Adopt the Surveillance MVP (S1 + S3a + S4) and pilot in 3 provinces (Gauteng, Western Cape, KZN) for 6 months. Approximate pilot budget: ~R157,000 operating + ~R80,000 IT setup. Lead agency: NICD as national coordinator.

  • Weeks 1–2: S4 dashboard live; S3a LIS configuration begins.
  • Months 1–3: S1 IT connector built and tested; S4 MVD workshop with PIH.
  • Month 6: Evaluate against (a) completeness of NHLS severe results in NMC and (b) cluster-detection latency.
  • Month 9: Add S3b sentinel toxicology site, funded from a separate research-surveillance stream.

The coordination side of the same system — how NICD, EHPs, DALRRD, and provincial response teams act on the improved signal — is covered in the Coordination brief. The product-specific regulatory action that S3b makes possible is the subject of the Terbufos brief.

item.title: Policy Brief 3: Restricting or Banning Terbufos in South Africa
item.dc:creator: D2P Project Team

ImportantFor Decision-Makers

Target audience: DALRRD Pesticide Registrar, Ministerial Advisory Committee (MAC), National Department of Health (NDoH), Department of Trade, Industry & Competition (substitution support).

Companion briefs: Surveillance · Coordination.

Status: DRAFT. One genuine SA evidence gap remains (the adult live-patient attributable fraction, resolved only by Surveillance Option S3b). The other quantitative inputs — market volume, yield impact, substitute hazard, substitute pricing, enforcement cost — are not epistemic gaps: they are either administrative numbers DALRRD can pull, or values defensibly anchored to the EU/US/Sri Lanka evidence base (see §2b and Interim assumptions).

1. Policy question

Should South Africa restrict the use of terbufos, or ban it outright as a registered agricultural pesticide?

2. Public health problem

Terbufos is a WHO Class Ia (“Extremely Hazardous”) organophosphate insecticide.1 It is acutely toxic via oral, dermal, and inhalation routes, with a published rat oral LD50 of 1.6–4.5 mg/kg23 — placing it among the most acutely toxic active ingredients still in commercial use anywhere. It acts via irreversible cholinesterase inhibition; sub-gram doses are lethal in adults and very small quantities are lethal in children.

South African evidence base. Davies et al. (2023), reviewing paediatric pesticide deaths in South Africa, identified terbufos and methamidophos as the dominant agents in fatal childhood pesticide poisoning, with most deaths occurring after ingestion of granular formulations diverted into the informal “street-pesticide” market.4 This is corroborated by NICD/NMC clinical case reports and by the public-health record of mass-poisoning events in 2022–2024 linked to informally-sold granular OP pesticides.5 A formal case series with attributed agent breakdown across NMC + NHLS + forensic toxicology has not yet been compiled and is the single most important evidence-gap item to retire (see open items in the Parameters Hub, TBF-2).

The public-health case rests on three claims:

  1. High intrinsic toxicity at sub-gram doses — settled science (WHO Class Ia; rat oral LD50 1.6–4.5 mg/kg).67
  2. Disproportionate contribution to severe and fatal poisonings — supported in paediatric SA data (Davies 2023);8 adult attributable fraction is not yet quantified pending live-patient chemical toxicology (Surveillance Option S3b).
  3. High substitutability for its primary use cases (soil insect / stalk borer / nematode control in maize and other field crops) — registered substitutes exist (see §5), but SA-specific yield-impact modelling is not yet done (open item TBF-3).

2b. International natural-experiment evidence

South Africa does not have to model terbufos withdrawal from first principles. Three relevant natural experiments have already been run:

  • Sri Lanka (1995–2011). Sequential bans on WHO Class I organophosphates reduced pesticide-suicide mortality by ~50 % and total suicide mortality by ~21 %, without compensating method substitution.9 Each banned single agent typically accounted for 20–40 % of fatal pesticide poisonings in the period immediately before its withdrawal.
  • Bangladesh, Nepal, India. Class Ia/Ib restrictions show the same direction and order of magnitude.
  • EU (2009) and US EPA (2006). Terbufos was withdrawn (EU) or moved to RUP-only with granular formulations voluntarily cancelled (US). No documented maize-yield collapse in any producer state.

The Sri Lanka studies are the strongest available evidence that single-agent Class Ia withdrawal does retire most of that agent’s attributable fatal burden, and does not redistribute it to substitute agents at the same lethality. SA paediatric data (Davies 2023) is independently consistent with terbufos sitting in the 20–40 % attributable bracket.

NoteWhat DALRRD action delivers — and to whom

DALRRD itself bears ~R0 of the R2.34B annual burden. That cost is carried by NDoH (~R70M hospital), NHLS (~R10M lab), and most heavily by households (~R2.26B in out-of-pocket costs and lost lifetime earnings). DALRRD nevertheless holds the only lever — registration, restriction, recall — that prevents the underlying exposure in the first place. A regulatory action borne by DALRRD (~R1–3M/year of additional enforcement and inspectorate capacity) therefore retires household-borne mortality cost at a leverage ratio of roughly 1 : 500: one rand of regulatory spend averts five hundred rand of household income loss. For DALRRD this is not a cost — it is the single highest-impact use of regulatory authority on the SADC pesticide-poisoning portfolio.

Terbufos-specific status quo:

Item Status Evidence basis

WHO classification Class Ia (Extremely Hazardous) WHO Recommended Classification of Pesticides by Hazard10

Why act now?

  • 2022–2024 mass-poisoning events placed terbufos in the public and political spotlight,14 creating a window for regulatory action that may not recur.
  • The EU removed terbufos from its approved list more than a decade ago; South Africa is an outlier among middle-income agricultural exporters in still permitting it.
  • The Surveillance + Coordination investments give DALRRD, for the first time, the institutional pathway to act on a single-product signal.

4. Root cause analysis

The drivers cluster into intrinsic-hazard, formulation, market, attribution-evidence, and substitution-readiness causes. Three of five are addressed by regulatory action on terbufos itself; R4 by the Surveillance brief; R5 by DALRRD–grain industry co-design.

5. Policy options

Option T1 — No change (status quo)

Terbufos remains registered under existing conditions. Relies on general pesticide-handling regulations and clinician/EHP-led NMC notifications to detect harm. This is the implicit decision if no regulatory action is taken.

Option T2 — Tighter restriction (★ recommended interim)

A bundle of measures short of an outright ban:

  • Formulation restriction. Withdraw granular formulations that visually resemble food/seed; allow only encapsulated or liquid formulations dispensed via licensed agricultural distributors.
  • Restricted-use product (RUP) designation. Sales only to certified applicators against a logged transaction; no informal-market sales.
  • Mandatory point-of-sale labelling and lockable container requirement.
  • Quarterly DALRRD audit of distributor records, with NICD→DALRRD intelligence feed (see Coordination brief Option C3) flagging geographies of concern.
  • Sunset clause. Conditional 24-month re-registration; if NICD-attributed serious-poisoning cases (from S3b toxicology, once operational) do not decline by a pre-agreed margin, automatic transition to Option T3.

Cost: principally regulatory and enforcement. [Evidence gap: DALRRD inspectorate cost model for RUP enforcement.] Implementation: 6–12 months.

Option T3 — Full ban / phase-out

Cancel terbufos product registrations under the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act. Phase-out window (12–24 months) to allow substitute uptake and product clearance. Aligns South Africa with the EU position.

Trade-offs to manage:

  • Crop-yield impact on maize. [Evidence gap: SA-specific yield modelling under leading substitute actives; requires DALRRD + grain-industry collaboration.]
  • Substitute toxicity profile. Some substitutes (e.g. fipronil, certain neonicotinoids) carry their own ecological and human-health concerns. [Evidence gap: SA-specific comparative hazard assessment.]
  • Smallholder access. Substitutes may be more expensive or harder to access at smallholder scale. [Evidence gap: substitute pricing and accessibility.]
  • Compliance / black-market risk. A poorly-enforced ban can drive demand to unregulated supply. Mitigated by DALRRD inspectorate capacity (Coordination C3) and by Option T2 acting as a 24-month stepping stone.

Cost: regulatory cost low; market-transition cost concentrated on growers and distributors. [Evidence gap.] Implementation: 12–24 months.

6. Decision tree — terbufos regulatory choices

How to read the tree. Public-health, agricultural, and implementation consequences are shown separately rather than collapsed into a single utility. T1 is best for agriculture and implementation but worst for public health. T3 is best for public health but loads risk onto the agricultural and implementation arms. T2 is a calibrated middle path with a built-in evaluation gate at 24 months that mechanically escalates to T3 if the public-health gain is insufficient.

Quantitative anchor (bracketed estimate)

Using the shared parameter set and the Sri Lanka attributable-fraction bracket:

  • Terbufos attributable fraction of fatal SA pesticide poisonings: 20–35 % (point ~25 %), anchored to Sri Lanka single-agent withdrawal studies and consistent with Davies 2023 paediatric SA dominance.1516
  • Applied to ~1,500 fatal pesticide-poisoning deaths/yr → ~300–500 deaths/yr are plausibly terbufos-attributable.
  • Option T3 (full withdrawal) at Sri Lanka-class substitution-incompleteness (60–80 % of attributable burden actually retired) → ~200–400 deaths/yr averted.
  • Option T2 (formulation restriction + RUP + audit), partial coverage of the informal-market diversion pathway only → ~80–180 deaths/yr averted, with the 24-month evaluation gate sized to detect this signal.

This is a bracketed working estimate, not a point claim. The bracket is wide on purpose. The single piece of evidence that would tighten it — a live-patient adult attributable fraction — is the Surveillance Option S3b deliverable at month 12. Decision-makers should not wait for it: the lower end of the bracket alone (~200 deaths/yr) at a regulatory cost of ~R1–3M/yr gives a leverage ratio of approximately 1 : 500 on household-borne mortality cost — the case for action is robust across the full bracket.

7. Implementation considerations

Issue Status Mitigation
Regulatory authority DALRRD has full authority under the Act None required
Pesticide registration cancellation process Established administrative pathway Standard DALRRD process
Attributable-fraction evidence [Evidence gap] Stand up Surveillance Option S3b at 1 sentinel site within 12 months
Yield-impact evidence [Evidence gap] Commission grain-industry / ARC modelling alongside Option T2
Substitute hazard profile [Evidence gap] DALRRD comparative hazard review at registration
Smallholder access to substitutes [Evidence gap] Grower advisory + transition subsidy via DALRRD
Compliance / black-market risk High under T3 if poorly enforced T2 as a 24-month stepping stone; Coordination C3 intelligence feed
Stakeholder consultation Required DALRRD + grain industry + civil-society public-comment process

Institutional responsibilities. DALRRD leads regulatory action. NDoH/NICD supplies the attributable-harm evidence base (via Surveillance S3b and Coordination C3). DTIC and Agriculture sector bodies lead substitution support. Civil-society and grower organisations participate in formal consultation.

8. Recommended next step

Adopt Option T2 immediately as an interim measure, with a hard-coded 24-month evaluation gate that escalates to Option T3 unless a pre-agreed reduction in attributable serious-poisoning cases is demonstrated.

Concretely:

  1. Within 3 months. DALRRD gazette the formulation restriction, RUP designation, distributor audit, and lockable-container requirement.
  2. Within 6 months. NICD operationalises the Coordination Option C3 NICD→DALRRD intelligence feed with quarterly terbufos-specific reporting.
  3. Within 12 months. Surveillance Option S3b sentinel live-patient chemical toxicology site operational, producing the attributable-fraction evidence base.
  4. Within 24 months. Joint NDoH–DALRRD review against pre-agreed reduction target → escalate to Option T3 if target missed, retain Option T2 if met.
  5. In parallel. Commission the four explicit [Evidence gap] work items (market volume, attributable fraction, yield-impact, substitute hazard) to retire the uncertainty that today prevents a clean cost–benefit calculation.

This is the option that takes the strongest public-health action immediately compatible with the evidence on hand, while building the evidence base needed to defend a full ban on its merits at the 24-month gate.

item.title: Pesticide Poisoning Surveillance Concept Note
item.dc:creator: D2P Project Team
item.description:
1 Executive Summary

This concept note outlines a comprehensive framework for improving pesticide poisoning surveillance in South Africa. Building on lessons learned from the National Notifiable Medical Conditions (NMC) system, NHLS laboratory data, and the Poisons Information Helpline, we propose an integrated surveillance approach that:

  1. Links existing data streams without creating new parallel systems
  2. Automates notification workflows to reduce reporting delays
  3. Enables hotspot detection through spatial and temporal clustering analysis
  4. Supports rapid public health response via clear escalation protocols
NoteStatus

This is a DRAFT concept note (Version 3, dated 11 August 2025). The framework is designed to be piloted in 2–3 provinces before national rollout.

2 Background: The Surveillance Gap

2.1 Current System Architecture

South Africa has three parallel data sources for pesticide poisoning, but they operate independently:

What this diagram shows. Five gaps in the current state:

  1. NICD/NMC is the source of truth for case notifications but receives only the clinician-completed NMC stream (~690/year) — a fraction of the true burden.
  2. The NHLS laboratory holds two distinct streams: (a) BChE assays on live patients (~2,000 severe results/year, capability exists) and (b) Chemical toxicology — qualitative/quantitative pesticide assays which NHLS currently performs post-mortem only. Live-patient chemical toxicology is not yet available (see Component 6).
  3. Neither NHLS stream feeds NICD in a structured way. BChE has no automated notification; chemical toxicology is not yet generated on living patients at all.
  4. The EHP arm exists but does not close the loop. When an NMC notification is filed, an SMS reaches the local EHP, who is mandated to investigate — but neither the investigation outcome nor the informal DALRRD referral is recorded back on NMC, and DALRRD’s regulatory action (if any) is fed back to the EHP at best, never to NICD or the clinician.
  5. PIH consultations are not captured against a minimum viable dataset, so the ~9,000 calls/year cannot be aggregated, geocoded, or matched to NICD cases.

2.2 Missed Opportunities

From 2020–2024:

  • ~3,450 NMC notifications were filed, but at least ~10,000 severe BChE inhibitions were detected in NHLS labs
  • Gap of ~6,550 cases that should have triggered public health investigation
  • No clustering analysis to identify hotspots (e.g., contaminated food sources, illegal pesticide sales)

3 Proposed Framework

3.1 Design Principles

  1. Integration over duplication: Link existing systems rather than building new infrastructure
  2. Automation over manual reporting: Use laboratory triggers and structured data flows
  3. Timeliness over completeness: Prioritize rapid detection for actionable hotspots
  4. Scalability: Start with pilot provinces, expand based on evidence

3.2 System Architecture

3.3 Key Components

3.3.1 1. Laboratory-Triggered Surveillance (Option 3)

Implementation:

  • Configure NHLS Laboratory Information System (LIS) to flag BChE results < 50% of normal
  • Auto-generate notification to NICD with:
    • Patient demographics (age, sex, facility)
    • BChE value and normal range
    • Test date and time
  • Notification sent within 24 hours of result validation

Data flow:

NHLS LIS → HL7 message → NICD middleware → NMC database → Surveillance dashboard

Cost: ~R55,000/year (mostly IT staff time for configuration)

3.3.2 2. Poisons Information Helpline Integration (Option 4)

Implementation:

  • PIH generates quarterly reports summarizing:
    • Total pesticide-related calls
    • Age/sex distribution
    • Geographic distribution (by referring facility)
    • Severity classification (minor, moderate, severe)
    • Suspected pesticide type
  • Reports sent to NICD for temporal trend analysis

Data flow:

PIH call log → Quarterly extraction → Excel/CSV → Email to NICD → Manual review

Cost: ~R62,000/year (PIH analyst time)

3.3.3 3. Inter-Agency Data Sharing (Options 1–2)

Implementation:

  • Formalize Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) between:
    • NICD ↔︎ NHLS (laboratory data sharing)
    • NICD ↔︎ PIH (clinical toxicology data)
    • NICD ↔︎ DALRRD (pesticide registration and use data)
    • NICD ↔︎ SAPS (forensic toxicology for intentional poisonings)
  • Establish data governance framework:
    • What data are shared (minimum dataset)
    • How often (weekly, monthly, on-demand)
    • Privacy safeguards (de-identification, access controls)

Legal basis: Section 90 of the National Health Act (2003) allows inter-agency sharing for public health purposes

Cost: ~R80,000/year (legal review, MOU development, ongoing liaison)

3.3.4 4. Hotspot Detection Algorithm

Method:

Use space-time permutation scan statistic (SaTScan software) to detect clusters of:

  • Higher-than-expected case counts
  • In defined geographic areas (district or sub-district level)
  • Within defined time windows (2-week rolling window)

Implementation:

  • Run weekly on aggregated case data (NMC + BChE auto-notifications + PIH reports)
  • Generate alerts when:
    • Relative risk > 2.0 (cluster has 2× expected cases)
    • P-value < 0.05
    • Cluster includes ≥3 cases

Response protocol:

  1. Alert sent to provincial surveillance officer
  2. Officer reviews cluster for plausibility (ruling out data artifacts)
  3. If plausible, initiate field investigation within 72 hours

Cost: Included in Option 5 (~R40,000/year for analyst time)

4 Implementation Roadmap

4.1 Phase 1: Pilot (Months 1–6)

Pilot provinces: Gauteng, Western Cape, KwaZulu-Natal

Activities:

  1. Configure NHLS auto-notifications for pilot provinces
  2. Establish PIH quarterly reporting workflow
  3. Train provincial surveillance officers on hotspot response
  4. Develop standard operating procedures (SOPs)

Milestones:

  • Month 2: First auto-notification sent
  • Month 3: First PIH quarterly report delivered
  • Month 4: First cluster alert (if any)
  • Month 6: Pilot evaluation and refinement

4.2 Phase 2: National Rollout (Months 7–12)

Activities:

  1. Expand NHLS auto-notifications to all provinces
  2. Finalize MOUs for inter-agency data sharing
  3. Deploy SaTScan algorithm for weekly cluster detection
  4. Conduct national training for provincial teams

Milestones:

  • Month 9: All provinces receiving auto-notifications
  • Month 10: First national clustering analysis
  • Month 12: System fully operational

4.3 Phase 3: Evaluation (Months 13–24)

Metrics:

  1. Timeliness: Median time from exposure to notification
  2. Completeness: % of severe BChE inhibitions with corresponding NMC notifications
  3. Sensitivity: % of known outbreaks detected by cluster algorithm
  4. Response: % of clusters investigated within 72 hours
  5. Impact: Change in hospitalization rates in hotspot areas

5 Governance and Oversight

5.1 Roles and Responsibilities

Agency roles in the proposed framework
Agency Role
NICD Lead surveillance agency; cluster detection; national coordination
NHLS Laboratory testing; auto-notification configuration; quality assurance
PIH Clinical toxicology advice; quarterly reporting
Provincial DoH Field investigation; source control; environmental sampling
DALRRD Pesticide registration data; agricultural extension liaison
SAPS Forensics Intentional poisoning investigations; evidence collection

5.2 Coordination Mechanisms

  1. Quarterly steering committee meetings (NICD, NHLS, PIH, provincial representatives)
  2. Monthly technical working group calls (analysts and IT staff)
  3. Annual review and planning workshop

6 Budget Summary

Estimated annual costs for integrated surveillance framework
Component Annual Cost (ZAR) Notes
NHLS auto-notifications 55,000 IT staff time for LIS configuration
PIH quarterly reports 62,000 Analyst time for data extraction
Inter-agency MOUs 80,000 Legal review and liaison
Cluster detection 40,000 Analyst time for SaTScan runs
Total (Full Package) 237,000 All four options combined

7 Limitations and Risks

WarningKey Assumptions

This framework assumes:

  1. NHLS LIS can be configured for auto-notifications (confirmed as technically feasible)
  2. PIH has capacity to generate quarterly reports (requires dedicated analyst time)
  3. Provincial teams have resources for field investigations (may require additional funding)
  4. Legal basis is sufficient — no new legislation required (confirmed by legal review)

Risks:

  • Low uptake of BChE testing: If clinicians don’t order tests, laboratory triggers won’t fire
  • Data quality issues: Incomplete or incorrect demographic data may hinder hotspot detection
  • Response capacity constraints: Provincial teams may lack vehicles, sampling equipment, or staff time

8 Next Steps

  1. Secure funding for pilot phase (~R120,000 for 6 months)
  2. Finalize MOUs with NHLS and PIH (Month 1)
  3. Configure NHLS auto-notifications for pilot provinces (Months 1–2)
  4. Train provincial surveillance officers (Month 2)
  5. Launch pilot (Month 3)
  6. Evaluate and refine (Month 6)

9 References

  1. National Institute for Communicable Diseases. National Notifiable Medical Conditions Surveillance System Annual Report 2020–2024.
  2. NHLS Laboratory Information Services. Butyrylcholinesterase Testing Data 2020–2024.
  3. Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital. Poisons Information Helpline Annual Report 2019.
  4. Kulldorff M. SaTScan User Guide for Version 10.0. 2021.
  5. National Health Act No. 61 of 2003, Section 90 (Inter-Agency Data Sharing for Public Health).
